opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that distinction matters more than people sometimes realize. When we say "model," in the classical machine learning sense, we usually mean a fairly well-defined mathematical object: you have some parameters, you have a training procedure, and you have a mapping from inputs to outputs. You can study its generalization, its calibration, its failure modes, and you have a reasonably clean story about what it is.

But when you look at how large language models are actually deployed today, that story starts to break down. What a user interacts with is rarely just the raw weights. There's a system prompt, there's often retrieval, there are safety filters on the input and output, there's tool use, sometimes multiple model calls chained together, decoding choices, and then a whole layer of product decisions on top. And all of that gets updated over time, sometimes without much visibility to the people using it. So what you're really interacting with is a system, a composition of components, and the behavior you observe is a property of that whole composition, not just the underlying network.

That has real consequences, especially for evaluation, which is a lot of what my group thinks about. If you benchmark "the model" and then make claims about how it'll behave in the world, you may be measuring the wrong object. The same base model wrapped in two different systems can behave quite differently on safety, on fairness, on reliability. And conversely, some failures that look like model failures are really system-level failures: an interaction between retrieval and generation, or a filter that triggers in unexpected ways.

So I tend to encourage people to be explicit about what the unit of analysis is. If you care about scientific questions, like what capabilities emerge from scale, or how representations are learned, then thinking at the model level makes sense. But if you care about trustworthiness, about deployment, about the harms or benefits people actually experience, then you need to think at the system level, and that means borrowing ideas from systems engineering, from software testing, even from how we evaluate sociotechnical systems more broadly. It also changes questions of accountability: who's responsible for a behavior when it emerges from the interaction of several components built by different people?

I'd say the field is still catching up to that shift. A lot of our measurement tools were designed for the model view, and we're now trying to figure out what rigorous evaluation looks like when the thing we're evaluating is this larger, evolving system.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes that deployed LLMs are composed of prompts, retrieval, filters, tools, and product choices, and that users interact with the resulting system rather than just the model weights.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is actually one of the more important framing questions right now, and it's one I've been wrestling with a lot. When we say "model," we usually mean the thing that comes out of training, the weights, the function that maps inputs to outputs. And a lot of our evaluation tradition in machine learning is built around that object. You hold out a test set, you measure accuracy, you report a number, and that number is supposed to characterize the model.

But the thing people actually interact with, when they open up ChatGPT or Claude or whatever it is, is not that object. It's a system. There's a system prompt, there's retrieval, there's tool use, there's the sampling strategy, there's the safety filters sitting on top, there's the UI that shapes how people phrase their questions. And often the pieces change independently of each other. The underlying weights might be the same for months while everything around them shifts, and the behavior you observe shifts with it.

So the distinction matters for a few reasons. One is reproducibility. If I publish a benchmark result against "GPT-4" or some named model, what did I actually evaluate? The weights through a particular API, at a particular time, with a particular decoding configuration. If you can't pin that down, the claim is kind of unanchored. We've seen this in our own work where results drift over time and it's genuinely unclear whether that's the model changing or the scaffolding changing.

The second reason is that a lot of the properties we care about, reliability, safety, fairness, those are really properties of the system, not the model. A model might have some bias in its base behavior, and then a classifier on top of it mitigates that in deployment. Is the system fair? Maybe. Is the model fair? That's a different question, and depending on who you are, a researcher, a regulator, a user, you might care about one or the other. If you're thinking about open weights that get redeployed in a hundred different contexts, the model-level properties matter a lot. If you're thinking about harm to a specific user population, the system-level properties are what matter.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that the system view forces you to think about the human in the loop. The person using it is part of the system. How they prompt, how they interpret outputs, whether they verify things. A lot of what we call model failures are really interaction failures, and you can't see those if you're only looking at the weights in isolation.

So my own position has shifted toward saying: be explicit about which one you're talking about. If you're doing science, you often want to isolate the model so you can make controlled claims. If you're making claims about impact or deployment, you have to evaluate the system, and you have to be honest that your result is tied to a configuration that may not exist next month. The confusion comes when people measure one and make claims about the other.

r001.rationale: The response stresses that deployed LLMs are systems and that deployment claims should evaluate the system, but it also preserves model-level evaluation and says to be explicit about which one is being discussed. It does not characterize LLMs primarily as systems rather than models.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction matters because what we interact with is usually more than the model itself. The model is one component: it takes some input and produces some output. But when you use an LLM through a product, there may be instructions around it, retrieval, tools it can call, and filters on what comes back. All of those pieces shape the behavior you see.

So if we ask, “Is this reliable? Is it safe?” we have to be clear about what we’re evaluating. A property we measure in the model doesn’t necessarily carry over to the whole system. And the system might have safeguards that make it behave quite differently from the underlying model.

That doesn’t mean evaluating the model isn’t useful. It means there are different levels of analysis. Ultimately, if we care about the impact on a person using it, we need to evaluate the system they actually encounter, in the context where they’re using it.

r001.rationale: The response treats the model as one component and emphasizes that an LLM product’s behavior comes from the broader system, which is what users encounter and should evaluate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a useful distinction because the model is really just one component of what people interact with. You have this trained neural network that takes some input and produces an output. But when you use an application built around it, there may also be a system prompt, retrieval, tools, filters, and some logic that decides how those pieces work together. That whole thing is the system.

And that matters when we talk about capabilities or trustworthiness. If you evaluate the model in isolation, you’ve learned something, but you haven’t necessarily learned how the application behaves. Adding retrieval might help with some factual questions, for example, but now the behavior also depends on what gets retrieved and how the model uses it.

So I would ask: What exactly are we making a claim about? Is it the underlying model, or is it the system that a person actually uses? Both are useful objects of study, but the evidence you need to support a claim can be quite different.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the underlying model from the larger application system, but treats both as useful objects of study rather than characterizing LLMs primarily as systems.
